title: Where Private Capital is Being Deployed
summary: LPL Research looks beyond AI IPOs to explore where private capital may be headed next, from infrastructure and defense to healthcare.
body_markdown:
# After the AI IPOs: Where Private Capital Goes Next


[Michael McClain](https://www.lpl.com/research/research-team/michael-mcclain.html) | Alternative Investment Research Analyst and Due Diligence


Last Updated: November 18, 2026


According to PitchBook, global private equity deal values reached $499 billion in the third quarter, up nearly 8% from the prior quarter. Exit activity also strengthened, with global exit value approaching $482 billion and U.S. exit value rising 51%.


Artificial intelligence (AI) remains a major driver of activity, while the Anthropic initial public offering (IPO) will provide another important test for the reopening IPO market. However, capital is also beginning to move beyond the largest AI companies and into the infrastructure, industries, and services supporting the broader technology buildout. That shift matters because private markets need more than new investment activity, as managers must also be able to sell existing holdings, return capital to limited partners, and raise and deploy new funds. After several years of limited exits and weak distributions, an improving liquidity environment could help restart that cycle. The backlog has not disappeared. U.S. venture capital calls exceeded distributions by $36.8 billion in the first quarter of 2026, leaving substantial capital tied up in private portfolios.


## AI Is Still Winning, but the Opportunity Is Broadening


- AI represented 65% of total venture deal value in 2025, according to PitchBook; however, AI is increasingly too broad a label. The first phase rewarded semiconductors and the companies building frontier AI models. The next phase has favored the infrastructure and businesses surrounding those models, such as data centers, electrical equipment, power generation, and cooling systems.
- That represents an important evolution, as private market investors do not necessarily need to determine which large-language model ultimately wins. They can potentially own the infrastructure that almost every model requires.


## Defense Industry Is Attracting Capital


- Defense represents another increasingly important destination. Private equity completed 128 defense deals through September 2026, already exceeding the 89 completed during all of 2025, according to PitchBook.
- This theme increasingly intersects with AI through autonomous systems, drones, cybersecurity, satellites, sensors, and software-defined defense systems. For private equity managers, these businesses can also fit a traditional value-creation playbook: acquire specialized suppliers, invest in capacity, consolidate markets, and potentially sell larger platforms to strategic buyers or other sponsors.


## Healthcare Offers a Different AI Opportunity


- Healthcare could represent another destination for private capital, but for a somewhat different reason. Rather than simply investing in companies selling AI, private equity can own established businesses that use AI to improve their economics.
- Healthcare IT, pharmaceutical services, medical technology, and healthcare services businesses may be able to automate administrative functions such as documentation, scheduling, billing, and customer service. The underlying company does not need AI to create explosive revenue growth. If technology reduces labor costs or improves productivity, AI can become a margin enhancement tool. For private equity, that may be a more familiar proposition: buy an established business, improve operations, and expand operating margins.


## Software Revisited


- One consequence of the AI boom has been greater uncertainty around traditional software. The question is no longer simply whether a software company has recurring revenue; rather, investors increasingly need to determine whether AI strengthens its competitive advantage or makes its product easier to replicate.
- That could ultimately create opportunity if valuations reset; however, private equity investors will need to distinguish between companies that are temporarily cheaper because investors are nervous about an unknown AI disruption versus companies whose competitive position has been permanently altered.


## LPL Research Takeaway


AI may be helping reopen the private market cycle, but it’s unlikely to be the cycle’s only beneficiary. As exits return capital to investors, new commitments are beginning to fund a wider opportunity set, from data centers and power generation to defense, healthcare, and robotics. Capital is also concentrating among larger managers, with the 10 largest funds expected to attract more than 40% of private equity fundraising in 2026. Scale can help finance these opportunities, but the ability to create value will matter more than fund size alone. For advisors, the key is to look beyond the AI label. The more durable opportunity may be found in businesses that provide the infrastructure AI requires, apply the technology to improve productivity, or benefit from the investment cycle surrounding it. As the theme expands, manager selection, entry valuation, and a credible path to liquidity will remain more important than chasing the next headline IPO.
